SONAR , the freight market intelligence platform, has added intermodal rates to Rate Intelligence, giving shippers, freight brokers and carriers a new way to evaluate truckload-to-intermodal conversion potential on any lane.
Users can now view intermodal contract and spot rates, compare them side by side with van pricing, and estimate the savings per load from converting truckload freight to intermodal. On the Chicago-to-Elizabeth, New Jersey lane, for example, intermodal contract pricing runs 21.1% below van contract, about $593 per load.
At a glance
What: Intermodal rates, ramps, trends and Conversion Savings inside SONAR Rate Intelligence
Who it’s for: Shippers, freight brokers, 3PLs and carriers evaluating mode shifts
Data included: Intermodal contract rates, intermodal spot rates on covered corridors, rate and volume trends
How to access: Select intermodal as an equipment type, or drill into it from any van lane
Available: October 2026, for Rate Intelligence users
What can you do with intermodal in SONAR Rate Intelligence?
See intermodal pricing. View intermodal contract rates, plus intermodal spot rates where coverage is available.
Know the resolved lane. See the resolved intermodal lane, including suggested in-gate and out-gate ramps and their distance from origin and destination.
Compare modes side by side. Line up intermodal and van pricing across rate per mile (RPM), flat rate, fuel surcharge, and month-over-month and year-over-year change.
Track trends. Review intermodal rate and volume trends over the last 12 months, in absolute or relative view.
Size the opportunity. Evaluate Conversion Savings, including estimated savings per load, total lane savings, intermodal volume and conversion potential. Enter your own rate and annual volume to personalize the math.
Work your way. Select intermodal directly as an equipment type, or drill into the intermodal view while researching a van lane.
Example: Chicago to Elizabeth, New Jersey intermodal vs. truckload
On the Chicago-to-Elizabeth lane, intermodal contract pricing runs about 21% below van contract, worth roughly $593 per load.
Rail miles: 808 average intermodal miles
In-gate ramp: Chicago 14th Street (Global I), Union Pacific, 1 mile from Chicago
Out-gate ramp: Norfolk Southern ramp in Elizabeth, New Jersey, 3 miles from Elizabeth
How the modes compare
Mode | Rate per mile | Flat rate | Month-over-month change
Intermodal contract | $2.77 | $2,220.92 | +7.66%
Van contract | $3.58 | $2,813.88 | +9.15%
Van spot | $3.92 | $3,081.12 | +6.52%
What the conversion view shows
Savings: Intermodal contract is 21.1% below van contract, or $592.96 per load.
Confidence: The intermodal contract rate of $2,220 sits within a $2,075 to $2,435 range, built on 46 observations over a 41-day lookback.
Volume: 283 domestic intermodal containers support the lane, and conversion potential is rated High .
Trend: Intermodal contract rates are up 11.55% year over year.
Figures reflect SONAR data at the time of publication.
Why does intermodal in Rate Intelligence matter?
Mode decisions no longer need a separate data source or a side spreadsheet.
Faster answers: Compare intermodal and truckload on the same lane, in the same workflow.
Clearer opportunities: Flag lanes where intermodal offers a real cost-saving alternative to truckload.
Stronger conversations: Bring conversion math, not guesses, to customer, carrier and procurement discussions.
Frequently asked questions
What is truckload-to-intermodal conversion?
Truckload-to-intermodal conversion means moving freight that travels by over-the-road truck onto rail in containers, with truck drayage at each end. Shippers typically convert longer-haul lanes to lower cost per load when transit time allows.
What intermodal data does SONAR Rate Intelligence include?
Rate Intelligence includes intermodal contract rates, intermodal spot rates on covered corridors, the resolved intermodal lane with in-gate and out-gate ramps, rate and volume trends, and Conversion Savings estimates.
How does SONAR calculate Conversion Savings?
Conversion Savings compares the van flat rate to the intermodal contract flat rate on the same lane. Savings per load is the difference between the two, and total lane savings applies that figure to the annual volume you enter.
Does every lane have intermodal spot rates?
No. SONAR’s intermodal spot index covers roughly 100 high-volume corridors. Lanes outside that set show intermodal contract rates for comparison.
How do I find intermodal rates in SONAR?
Select intermodal as the equipment type in Rate Intelligence, or open the intermodal view while researching a van lane. Saved intermodal lanes are labeled with an “I.”
Who should use intermodal rates in Rate Intelligence?
Shippers, freight brokers, 3PLs and carriers use it to test mode shifts, price lanes, support procurement and bid decisions, and identify lanes where intermodal can lower transportation costs.

source_document.body:
When the heads of three of the power sector’s biggest trade associations shared a stage at Experience POWER on Sept. 30, the most notable thing was how little they disagreed. Whether the question was data center backlash, grid security, or what to do about gas-plant emissions rules, the answer came back to the same point: The grid needs a lot more infrastructure, it will cost more than the old infrastructure did, and no regulatory shortcut will let the sector avoid either fact.
The session, “Inside the Issues,” was moderated by Mark W. Menezes, president and CEO of the United States Energy Association (USEA) . It brought together Jim Matheson, CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA) ; Tom Falcone, president of the Large Public Power Council (LPPC) ; and Rich Powell, CEO of the Clean Energy Buyers Association (CEBA) . Co-ops, the largest public power systems, and the corporate buyers that include the hyperscalers all feel load growth differently. They still arrived at similar conclusions.
Data Centers Have a Social License Problem
Falcone said that growth projections at today’s level did not exist three years ago, and that he would not have predicted them. Some LPPC members, he said, “have to double or triple in size over the next 10 years.” He also said that 18 months ago he would not have expected people to be coming to LPPC members and saying, “You shouldn’t be building this.” The members’ answer is consistent: “Hey, we serve the needs. We aren’t the ones permitting the projects. We aren’t the ones deciding the land use.”
Powell, whose members include the hyperscalers, was the bluntest about the risk. He said the data center industry has responded with a White House ratepayer protection pledge and voluntary commitments on costs and water, yet opposition has become a dominant narrative in many communities. His worry, he said, is whether data centers “end up in the place that nuclear power plants ended up 40 years ago,” a reference to the long moratoria on new nuclear construction. The industry is weighing a more concerted national push to show that data centers benefit communities through tax bases, jobs, and other community benefits, he said. “The burden right now is on the data center community to prove that to communities in a more profound way than they were doing before.”
Powell also made the case against building private power plants next to data centers. His members would prefer to buy from utilities, he said. “We like grids. Grids are good.” He added that he sees large co-located projects as a sign the grid could not serve a load in time, citing a Meta facility in Ohio that, he said, faced a seven-year wait for interconnection.
Security Rules Need One Standard
On the recent executive order directing utilities to identify equipment that could pose security risks, particularly equipment from adversary countries, all three leaders accepted that the threat is real. “There are actors out there that want to infiltrate our system,” Matheson said, though he urged regulators to rely on “actual, truthful, fact-based information, and not fear and rhetoric.” Powell asked that any requirements not be over-broad or discriminatory toward particular technologies.
Falcone offered the most specific prescription. Utilities cannot see their suppliers’ suppliers, he said, and asking each supplier to disclose that to roughly 1,500 registered entities is unworkable. He pointed to the nuclear industry and Europe, which he said use certification of origin handled by a single body. He also raised aggregation: Individual inverter-based resources may be too small to pose a risk, but enough of them together might. Falcone cited a news report, which he said appeared about six months before the panel, of about a dozen inverter-based resources being opened up and unauthorized communications equipment being found in every one. A patchwork won’t work, he said: “It can’t be 1,500 entities on the bulk electric system, each trying to solve the problems themselves.”
Flexible Load: Welcome in Theory, Hard to Sell
All three praised the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for not imposing a one-size-fits-all approach to large-load interconnection and for letting regional grid operators tailor their own rules. Falcone and Powell differed on how much the flexibility option will matter.
Falcone said one grid operator launched a product about six weeks before the panel that offers faster interconnection to flexible loads. He said that when LPPC members met with the operator, the question was whether anyone had signed up: “the answer is no.” A data center’s cost of interruption is so high, he said, that “you really don’t want flexible load. You want firm service.” He put it this way: “The amount of flexibility on the grid is determined by the buyer’s economics, not by the seller.” His conclusion: “There’s no magic bullet here.”
Powell did not dispute the economics but argued for a wider definition of flexibility. A buyer running high-value inference workloads may not curtail, he said, but could add energy storage or invest in virtual power plants that give the grid the same relief. He wants solutions “as performance-based, and technology and business-model neutral, as possible.”
Gas Rules and the Gas Bet
Matheson said the Environmental Protection Agency’s repeal of the Biden-era carbon capture requirement for existing coal and gas plants was a major win for cooperatives, who he said faced forced closures. But he warned that the rule’s efficiency requirement for new gas plants remains, and that NRECA’s outside consultants concluded it would limit combined-cycle plants to running only about 40% of the time.
Falcone argued the cost is the problem. A plant forced to run less means more plants. “It just makes the grid operate very inefficiently and raises costs without reducing carbon,” he said, adding that LPPC’s members span red and blue states. “We’re just for rules that work.”
Powell, who said he is a longtime carbon capture advocate, was candid about the technology’s status. “We do not in the United States today have a working carbon capture system up and running on a gas plant,” he said. Members such as Google have contracted for gas with capture, he said, and the first are scheduled to come online around 2030.
An audience question from a representative of Old Dominion Electric Cooperative on a possible gas overbuild brought out the shared worry. “Everybody’s betting on gas,” Matheson said, and “if you want to order a gas turbine, you can’t get one before 2032.” Falcone said fuel diversity protects the grid, but that as reliance on gas grows, redundancy, generally oil in a tank, costs money, and not every market has a revenue stream to pay for it. “The oil in the tank solves a lot of problems if you have a problem with a pipeline,” said Falcone. But for a for-profit generator, the logic is simple: “If you don’t pay me for it, I’m not going to do it,” he said. Powell questioned whether the country has an adequate framework for evaluating gas concentration risk, adding that the North American Electric Reliability Corporation has been calling for some kind of gas-electric coordination standard for years, along with reliability requirements for gas pipelines.
Permitting: From Briefings to Bill Text
The panel took place as a bipartisan Senate permitting package was expected to surface. Powell, citing briefings from the negotiators, described the outlines then circulating: faster environmental reviews, less litigation risk, protections against permits being pulled after construction starts, and long-haul transmission reform. Matheson said the consensus that Congress needs to act on permitting is stronger than at any point in his career. “Let’s take the win. Let’s move down the field. Let’s get some progress. We can live to fight another day,” he said, adding that he is a believer in taking “the partial loaf” when the full loaf isn’t available. Falcone was cautious: “Devil’s in the details, and we really need to see the bill text.”
The text arrived later that day. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act was introduced by Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee, and Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah), chair of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, along with ranking members Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.). According to the sponsors, the bill would let permitted projects keep their permits absent extraordinary circumstances, violations of law, or court order, and would require data centers to pay their transmission costs. The Bipartisan Policy Center (BPC), in an Oct. 2 explainer, described a 417-page bill that, among other provisions, would bar cost-shifting to other customers for new data centers of 20 MW or more. BPC said it expects a Senate cloture vote on the motion to proceed on Nov. 9 and that amendments are possible. CEBA issued a statement from Powell the same day calling the package “a generational opportunity to unleash abundant American energy.”
Who Pays
The session’s last exchange, prompted by a question about Pennsylvania’s infrastructure grade, brought the theme home. Falcone said LPPC members’ capital budgets have on average doubled in three years, which “means you need double the engineers and double the linemen and double the supply chain.” The sector will muddle through, he said, but the cost arrives either way. “Everybody has to pay more, and that’s an affordability challenge.”
Falcone then invited Powell to weigh in. “We are paying our way,” Powell said.
— Aaron Larson is executive editor of POWER.

Centerra Gold's Thompson Creek molybdenum mine in Idaho. Credit: Centerra Gold.
Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO October 8, 2026
Molybdenum is on course for a sixth consecutive year of supply deficit in 2027, setting the stage for record prices as strong demand meets a limited pipeline of new production, BMO Capital Markets says in a new report.
Global molybdenum demand climbed 8.5% to 358.2 million lb. in this year’s first half even as supply slipped 0.6% to 335.6 million lb., leaving a 22.6-million-lb. shortfall, according to data from the International Molybdenum Association cited by BMO.
Prices for the metal have soared about 43% to $41.97 (C$59.60) per lb. since Jan. 1, Daily Metal Prices data show. That makes molybdenum a “star performer,” BMO mining analysts George Heppel, Raj Ray and Helen Amos wrote in a report published Thursday.
As no new projects exist to lift output in the short term, the trend should continue in 2027, BMO says. Readily available inventories have been substantially depleted, leaving the market with limited buffers against further deficits, the bank says.
“With molybdenum demand growth looking strong and no major new sources of supply on the horizon, we believe that it is reasonable to expect the deficit to persist into 2027,” Heppel and his colleagues wrote.
“We now expect molybdenum to hit record highs in the coming year, something which is likely underappreciated by the metal market and wider investment community.”
Critical element
Molybdenum, a silvery-white element that’s used to strengthen steel and improve heat and corrosion resistance, is critical to sectors such as aerospace, energy and defence. China, the dominant global supplier, introduced export restrictions on the metal in February 2025 after U.S. President Donald Trump slapped tariffs on Chinese goods.
While incremental concentrate shipments from Myanmar may provide some relief at the margin, “these volumes are unlikely to materially alter the broader supply-demand balance,” the BMO analysts wrote. “In the absence of a more significant supply response, the market may ultimately need to rebalance through demand destruction in the medium term.”
However, demand for molybdenum is difficult to cut quickly. Molybdenum represents only a small share of the cost of many steel and alloy products, while providing key strength, corrosion resistance and high-temperature performance. Although elements such as chromium, nickel, vanadium, niobium and tungsten can replace it in some applications, there is no direct substitute across its broad range of uses.
As a result, “meaningful demand curtailment would likely require substantially higher prices than those seen historically,” the analysts wrote.
Cumulative shortfall
Global demand for the metal grew at a 4.4% annual rate between 2020 and 2025 to 671 million pounds.
Through the end of 2025, molybdenum’s global cumulative shortfall amounted to 108 million lb., BMO says. That’s equivalent to about two months of consumption.
About 60% of global molybdenum production comes as a byproduct of copper mining, particularly in Chile and Peru. Falling copper grades, deeper mines, water shortages, permitting delays, rising capital costs and years of underinvestment are limiting growth in those operations.
Chilean molybdenum production peaked in 2017 and has since declined, while South American supply overall has remained broadly flat for about a decade, BMO says.
While China has historically responded to molybdenum shortages by rapidly increasing production from primary mines, a similar response is unlikely this time, the bank says.
Resource depletion, tighter environmental and safety rules and a shift toward higher-value manufacturing have made Chinese mining less responsive to higher prices. Although large projects such as Zijin Mining’s Shapinggou are under construction, they aren’t expected to reach full output before around 2029. Until then, new Chinese supply should be limited.
Few options
China is also unlikely to solve the shortage through imports, according to the report.
Unlike antimony and tungsten, where China has been able to increase imports from flexible sources, there are few comparable external sources of molybdenum. Myanmar has increased shipments, but much of the material is low-grade ore rather than conventional molybdenum concentrate. Kazakhstan has also boosted output from copper mines, but BMO expects little further growth from the country.
More than 80% of molybdenum consumption is tied to metallurgical applications, including engineering and stainless steels. The metal is also widely used in oil and gas infrastructure, refining, power generation, chemical processing and other high-temperature and corrosion-resistant applications. Continued demand from energy infrastructure represents a key driver, BMO says.
A handful of producers and developers stand to benefit from the tightening market. BMO’s preferred miner is Centerra Gold (TSX: CG; NYSE: CGAU), whose molybdenum business includes the Thompson Creek mine in Idaho and the Langeloth processing facility in Pennsylvania. Thompson Creek is targeting production in mid-2027.
“Against tightening supply, Centerra offers one of the few listed avenues to a vertically integrated North American molybdenum platform,” Heppel, Ray and Amos wrote. The approaching completion of Thompson Creek’s capital program provides “a clear catalyst for greater market recognition.”
Among diversified U.S. miners, copper producer Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE: FCX) has the strongest molybdenum exposure through its Climax and Henderson mines in Colorado, BMO says. Molybdenum accounts for 7.3% of the company’s revenue, BMO says.

source_document.body:
Retailers that brought in holiday merchandise early to beat tariffs now face another challenge: selling it before storage costs and markdowns eat into profits. In this Q&A, Marcus Shen , CEO of B-Stock, a resale platform for excess and returned merchandise, discusses when to start clearing unsold goods, how to recover more value, and what retailers should do now to prepare for holiday returns.
What’s Related
Supply Chain 24/7: Many retailers brought holiday merchandise in early to get ahead of tariffs. What happens if that inventory does not sell as quickly as expected?
Marcus Shen : Retailers frontloaded inventory to get ahead of tariffs and supply-chain uncertainty, but that means more inventory is already sitting in the system before retailers have meaningful visibility into holiday demand.
The challenge isn't simply having too much inventory; it's having too much inventory too early, which increases the cost of being wrong.
And that cost compounds the longer inventory sits. It ties up working capital, adds warehousing and carrying costs, pressures margins as markdowns become necessary and increases the risk of obsolescence, particularly for seasonal, trend -driven and technology products. Eventually, what started as an inventory issue can become a cash-flow and balance-sheet issue.
The longer that inventory sits, the harder it becomes to recover its original value. Retailers need a clear plan for what happens when inventory doesn’t sell through as expected, including how quickly they can move excess into secondary channels and turn it back into cash. The companies that plan for that outcome upfront will have far more flexibility than those waiting until their warehouses are already full.
RELATED STORIES: How Early Is Too Early for Retailers to Buy Holiday Inventory? | Shoppers Plan Bigger Holiday Budgets, Demand Free Shipping
SC247: Are there particular products that are more likely to be overstocked this holiday season?
Shen: Apparel, electronics and home goods are categories I’d be watching closely. They’re largely discretionary purchases, and consumers have more flexibility to delay a purchase, trade down to a lower-priced option or shop through off-price and discount channels when budgets are tight. That makes demand harder to predict, particularly when retailers brought in inventory early.
Marcus Shen
The risk is that retailers end up with a gap between what they planned to sell and what consumers actually buy. The answer is to identify that risk early, segment inventory based on demand and expected recovery, and have multiple disposition options in place before excess inventory becomes a problem. Retailers need to be prepared to move inventory quickly if demand doesn’t materialize as expected, rather than waiting until the end of the season to figure out where it goes.
SC247: How long can retailers hold unsold merchandise before storage costs and declining value become a serious problem?
Shen: Every additional week inventory sits means more warehouse capacity consumed, more working capital tied up and a shorter window to make an efficient disposition decision.
The closer we get to the holidays, the more important inventory velocity becomes. Retailers need to know not just what they own, but how quickly they can move it if demand doesn't materialize.
“The closer we get to the holidays, the more important inventory velocity becomes. Retailers need to know not just what they own, but how quickly they can move it if demand doesn't materialize.”
SC247: At what point should a retailer consider discounting or selling excess inventory through the secondary market?
Shen: The time to think about secondary-market disposition is before you have a pileup of excess inventory. Retailers should evaluate their options before the holiday season ends and set clear triggers for when inventory should move out of the primary channel.
That doesn’t mean every slow-moving item needs to be pushed into the secondary market immediately. It means segmenting inventory based on velocity, seasonality, margin and expected recovery, and having multiple disposition channels ready to go. The goal isn’t simply to get the highest price per unit, it’s to optimize recovery, speed and control based on the retailer’s overall inventory position.
SC247: What are some common mistakes retailers make when trying to clear unsold holiday goods?
Shen: I think one of the biggest mistakes is waiting too long to make a plan. Retailers often try markdowns and promotions first, and by the time they start thinking about the secondary market, they’ve already lost time and potentially value.
The other mistake is treating all excess inventory the same. Every product has a different demand profile, seasonality and recovery opportunity. The retailers that are better prepared are the ones looking at those differences early and building multiple options for moving inventory. It’s not always about getting the highest price, it’s about finding the right balance of recovery, speed and control.
SC247: How can retailers recover as much value as possible without flooding the market or hurting their brands?
Shen: The key is to have a secondary-market strategy that gives you both scale and control. Retailers need enough buyer demand to create competition for their inventory, but they also need the ability to control who has access to it, where the merchandise goes and how it is sold.
That’s where the secondary market has changed. Today's infrastructure lets retailers reach large, vetted buyer networks and use competitive bidding so the market determines value, rather than relying on a single buyer to set the price. At the same time, retailers can put controls around the process, including buyer eligibility, resale restrictions, and visibility, to protect the brand and maintain channel integrity.
The goal is to move excess inventory quickly enough to avoid it becoming a balance-sheet liability, while maintaining the visibility and control needed to protect its value.
“Retailers have to be careful not to fall into a promotional trap. If consumers learn that waiting consistently means a better price, retailers can train them to delay purchases and wait for the next markdown.”
SC247: Could excess inventory lead to deeper discounts for shoppers this holiday season or early next year?
Shen: Yes, excess inventory could mean deeper discounts, particularly after the holidays. But retailers have to be careful not to fall into a promotional trap. If consumers learn that waiting consistently means a better price, retailers can train them to delay purchases and wait for the next markdown.
At the same time, holding inventory indefinitely isn’t really an option. Warehouses have finite capacity, new inventory needs to come in, and excess inventory ties up working capital. That’s especially challenging as consumers pull back on discretionary spending and increasingly turn to off-price and discount channels.
The answer isn’t simply to discount more aggressively. Retailers need to be thoughtful about which inventory they continue to support in the primary channel and which inventory should move into other channels before it becomes a bigger problem.
SC247: What should retailers be doing now to prepare for holiday returns and any merchandise left over after the season?
Shen: Retailers should be planning for the capacity to move inventory, not just the volume of returns they expect to receive. If frontloading leads to widespread overstock, many retailers could reach the same conclusion at the same time: we need to move inventory.
The challenge is that traditional secondary channels (jobbers, off-price retailers and other large purchasers) have finite buying capacity. If too many retailers turn to those channels at once, fewer buyers will be competing for that inventory, leading to longer dwell times and potentially lower recovery. Retailers should be building multiple disposition options now so they’re not relying on the same limited pool of buyers when everyone is trying to move inventory at once.

Retailers should evaluate their options before the holiday season ends and set clear triggers for when inventory should move out of the primary channel.
It means segmenting inventory based on velocity, seasonality, margin and expected recovery, and having multiple disposition channels ready to go.
The goal isn’t simply to get the highest price per unit, it’s to optimize recovery, speed and control based on the retailer’s overall inventory position.
The other mistake is treating all excess inventory the same.
The retailers that are better prepared are the ones looking at those differences early and building multiple options for moving inventory.
Retailers need enough buyer demand to create competition for their inventory, but they also need the ability to control who has access to it, where the merchandise goes and how it is sold.
The goal is to move excess inventory quickly enough to avoid it becoming a balance-sheet liability, while maintaining the visibility and control needed to protect its value.
If consumers learn that waiting consistently means a better price, retailers can train them to delay purchases and wait for the next markdown.”
SC247: Could excess inventory lead to deeper discounts for shoppers this holiday season or early next year?
Shen: Yes, excess inventory could mean deeper discounts, particularly after the holidays.
If consumers learn that waiting consistently means a better price, retailers can train them to delay purchases and wait for the next markdown.
At the same time, holding inventory indefinitely isn’t really an option.
Warehouses have finite capacity, new inventory needs to come in, and excess inventory ties up working capital.
Retailers need to be thoughtful about which inventory they continue to support in the primary channel and which inventory should move into other channels before it becomes a bigger problem.
Shen: Retailers should be planning for the capacity to move inventory, not just the volume of returns they expect to receive.
If frontloading leads to widespread overstock, many retailers could reach the same conclusion at the same time: we need to move inventory.
If too many retailers turn to those channels at once, fewer buyers will be competing for that inventory, leading to longer dwell times and potentially lower recovery.
Retailers should be building multiple disposition options now so they’re not relying on the same limited pool of buyers when everyone is trying to move inventory at once.

UPS is hiring 100,000 seasonal workers across hundreds of U.S. locations for the 2026 holiday shipping season . The company also announced changes to package security , tracking and pickup ahead of the rush.
What’s Related
Temporary employees will help sort, move and deliver packages. UPS said many applicants can receive a job offer in less than seven minutes, and some seasonal positions can lead to permanent jobs.
For shippers , the holiday preparations include a new Protected Delivery service that requires recipients to give drivers a PIN before receiving eligible packages. UPS also expects to deliver more than 4 billion packages equipped with radio frequency identification, or RFID , technology by the end of 2026.
The company is adding or updating automated facilities in Denver, St. Paul, Syracuse, and Portland. According to UPS’s announcement, the changes will help it maintain delivery performance during the year's busiest shipping period.

Hiring for the holidays
UPS’s hiring website says seasonal jobs typically run from October through December and have a set end date. Positions can be part-time or full-time, and some shifts start early in the morning or at midnight.
The jobs cover several parts of the delivery process. Warehouse workers sort and move packages, while driver helpers ride with delivery drivers and help deliver packages to customers without driving the truck.
Seasonal support drivers make deliveries using their own vehicles. UPS’s description says those workers receive mileage reimbursement, with a phone stipend available in some locations.
More advanced package tracking
RFID uses radio signals to identify tagged packages as they move through UPS facilities and vehicles. The company says the technology gives customers more precise tracking information.
In its April rollout announcement, UPS said it installed RFID sensing equipment in all of its U.S. package delivery vehicles and delivery facilities. At that time, the company also said packages shipped through more than 5,500 UPS Store locations carried the technology, including customer returns.
Kurt Goodwin, customer experience executive at electronics retailer Crutchfield, said the tracking helps reduce questions from customers. “For Crutchfield, that means fewer customer concerns, fewer tracking-related contacts, and greater confidence during the busiest shipping period of the year.”
A PIN before handoff
Protected Delivery adds a verification step at the doorstep: The recipient must provide a secure PIN before the driver releases the package. UPS describes the service as an option for eligible shipments, including high-value purchases and sensitive deliveries.
UPS is also adding pickup scheduling features and status alerts. Its holiday shipping options include returns through Happy Returns and local same-day or large-item deliveries through Roadie.

The Port of Savannah handled a record 504,015 TEUs in September, up 3.7% from a year earlier, as rising imports and weather-related cargo delays extended the peak shipping season, the Georgia Ports Authority said.
Loaded imports increased 5.5% compared with September 2025, leading the port’s container growth. GPA attributed the gains to strong consumer spending and typhoon-related delays at Asian ports that pushed peak-season shipments into September.
The result brought container volumes for the first quarter of GPA’s fiscal year to more than 1.5 million TEUs, an increase of 40,560 TEUs, or 2.7%, from the same period a year earlier. GPA said the quarter ranked second only to the first quarter of fiscal 2023. Volumes at the Appalachian Regional Port rose 13% during the quarter.
Terminal and road investments advance
GPA said its $1.6 billion renovation of Savannah’s Ocean Terminal is more than 60% complete. The project will increase the terminal’s annual container capacity from 200,000 TEUs to 1.75 million TEUs.
The authority also highlighted the Brampton Road Connector, a Georgia Department of Transportation project that opened in July. The road provides a third high-volume truck corridor to Garden City Terminal’s Gate 3, allowing trucks to avoid neighborhood roads and at-grade railroad crossings.
“The capital investments we’ve made are now paying off in service levels for our customers and fluidity for our trucking partners,” GPA President Kevin Price said.
GPA also said volumes will benefit from improving water conditions at the Panama Canal. According to the release, the Panama Canal Authority plans to restore capacity to a maximum of 10 Neopanamax vessel transits per day on Oct. 15, bringing total daily transit capacity for all vessel sizes to 33. The maximum draft for Neopanamax vessels stood at 49 feet as of Sept. 28.
Brunswick cargo declines despite machinery gains
At the Port of Brunswick, total roll-on/roll-off cargo fell 22% year over year to 43,415 units in September. Heavy machinery shipments rose nearly 12% to 3,754 units, compared with 3,359 a year earlier, but that growth did not offset the overall decline. GPA said global market conditions for vehicle manufacturers remained competitive as tariffs and rising interest rates have damped retail vehicle sales.

Virginia will receive up to $89.7 million in federal loans to add truck climbing lanes, improve highway ramps and replace aging bridges along Interstate 81, the U.S. Department of Transportation announced Oct. 7.
What’s Related
The financing will go to Virginia’s Commonwealth Transportation Board through the department’s Build America Bureau. The work targets congestion and safety problems along the interstate’s 325-mile route through Virginia, which carries 43% of the state’s interstate truck traffic, according to the federal announcement .
The package includes loans of up to $47.6 million and $42.1 million. Both use a federal rural transportation financing program that offers lower interest rates.
The loans will help pay for parts of Virginia’s broader $4 billion I-81 Corridor Improvement Program. Construction on many projects is already underway, with completion of the program slated for late 2035.
More room for trucks and merging traffic
Truck climbing lanes will be added in Washington and Augusta counties. These additional lanes give heavy trucks room to climb steep hills at lower speeds while passenger vehicles continue in the other lanes.
In Wythe County, the work includes extending exit ramps and adding merge lanes around Wytheville. The changes are intended to give drivers more room to accelerate when entering the interstate and slow down when leaving it.
The package also includes replacing aging bridges over Peppers Ferry Road and the northbound I-81 bridge over I-77. Together, the projects address several different sources of delays, from slow uphill traffic to tight highway merges.
Lower borrowing costs
The financing comes through the Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act, known as TIFIA. Its Rural Project Initiative offers eligible borrowers a fixed interest rate equal to half the comparable U.S. Treasury rate at the time a loan closes.
Traditional TIFIA loans charge the full comparable Treasury rate. The rural program can finance up to 49% of eligible project costs, helping borrowers reduce the cost of paying for road and bridge construction, according to the Build America Bureau .
Part of a larger highway overhaul
Virginia’s broader I-81 program includes 65 construction projects, along with changes to daily highway operations. Major work includes widening selected stretches from two lanes to three, adding truck climbing lanes, and extending lanes at interchanges, according to Virginia’s project website .
Other improvements include traffic cameras, digital message signs, safety service patrols, and better detour routes. Those changes are intended to help drivers respond to crashes and help crews clear incidents faster, alongside the larger construction projects.

Tesla is preparing a dedicated Tesla Semi service center in Las Vegas, according to a new building permit filed with Clark County, Nevada.
It’s one of the first concrete signs of the service network Tesla needs to support its electric Class 8 truck, which only entered volume production two weeks ago.
What the permit shows
The Clark County record (BD26-39451) describes the project in plain terms: “Tesla Semi Service Center. Tenant Improvement in new shell building.”
The site is 3780 N Las Vegas Blvd, part of the LV Logistics One industrial development on the northeast side of the valley, between I-15 and Nellis Air Force Base. The property owner is listed as L V Logistics One Property Owner LP, a Dallas-based entity, so Tesla is a tenant here and not building from scratch.

The application lists Tesla as the tenant and classifies the use as a “Repair Garage,” with the work type marked as a remodel under the 2024 building code. Its status is “Awaiting Plans,” which means the application is in but Tesla hasn’t submitted its construction drawings yet. So this isn’t opening next month.
The neighboring building in the same development, at 3790 N Las Vegas Blvd, gives a good idea of what Tesla is moving into. It’s a 152,256-square-foot logistics building completed in 2024 with 32-foot clear height, 20 dock-high doors, and a 122-foot truck court, according to its lease listing. That’s the kind of space you need to pull Class 8 tractors in and out all day.

Las Vegas sits on the I-15 corridor, one of the busiest freight routes in the West, linking the Southern California ports and warehouses of the Inland Empire to Las Vegas and on to Salt Lake City. Unfilled orders at U.S. factories rose 0.6% to $1,609.6 billion in August, and shipments stalled, the Census Bureau said in its Oct. 2 report on manufacturers’ shipments, inventories and orders . Backlogs have increased in 25 of the last 26 months. Transportation equipment accounted for $1,009.9 billion of the total and led the August increase.
Shipments were virtually unchanged at $658.6 billion, the first stall after eight monthly gains. New orders rose 0.1% to $663.5 billion. The ratio of unfilled orders to shipments rose to 6.87 from 6.81. Census does not adjust the figures for inflation.
Orders for motor vehicle bodies, parts and trailers rose 0.8%. Machinery orders rose 1.1%. Nondefense capital goods orders excluding aircraft rose 1.6%. Durable goods orders fell 0.1%, with transportation equipment down 0.7% and nondefense aircraft and parts down 4.3%.
A fabricated metal products respondent told the Institute for Supply Management the company has orders through year-end above forecast levels. “Our biggest challenge continues to be a severe shortage of workers, limiting our production output to meet demand. The second challenge is general availability of steel; the market is getting worse, and more production delays are expected as we gap out of needed material.”
Freight, diesel and steel cost more
ISM’s manufacturing index registered 54.5 in September, a tenth of a point below August, the group said in its Oct. 1 report . ISM said it was the ninth straight month of expansion after a 10-month contraction. The prices index climbed 6.8 points to 77.9, the largest move in the report. ISM said 58.6% of respondents reported paying higher prices, up from 46.2% in August.
Freight was on ISM’s list of commodities up in price for a seventh month. Diesel fuel was on it for a second. No commodity was reported down in price. The Energy Information Administration’s weekly benchmark diesel price, the figure most fuel surcharges use, set a record of $6.529 a gallon on Sept. 21 , FreightWaves’ John Kingston reported.
“The Prices Index reading is still being driven by (1) increases in steel and aluminum prices that impact the entire value chain, (2) tariffs applied to many imported goods and (3) increases in petroleum-based products as a result of the Middle East conflict,” said Susan Spence, chair of ISM’s Manufacturing Business Survey Committee.
A food, beverage and tobacco products respondent told ISM that “fuel costs are still affecting transportation costs and the overall cost of goods.” A machinery respondent said higher interest rates are slowing new construction and that “we also have to face up to the higher cost of components from overseas due to tariffs and freight rates.”
ISM’s inventories index fell 2 points to 48.6 in September, back in contraction. The customers’ inventories index slipped to 41.6, a 24th month in “too low” territory. “A ‘too low’ status for the Customers’ Inventories Index is usually considered positive for future production,” Spence said.
Canada tariffs and the August import jump
The August trade figures predate Canada’s retaliation. The U.S. goods deficit with Canada widened $4.1 billion to $7.1 billion as imports from Canada rose $4.6 billion to $37.1 billion, the Census Bureau and Bureau of Economic Analysis said. Ottawa put retaliatory tariffs of 15% to 50% on about C$27.6 billion in U.S. goods on Sept. 8, FreightWaves’ Noi Mahoney reported , matching U.S. duties after talks broke down in August.
“Canada tariffs have impacted cross-border costs and left our supply chain team scrambling — those supply chains took years to develop and nurture — hurting the very lead times government buyers are concerned about,” a machinery respondent said. That respondent said orders and delivery times had both doubled in semiconductors, electronics and government work.
Goods imports rose $17.2 billion to $342.2 billion in August, and the goods deficit widened $12.8 billion to $136.6 billion. Industrial supplies accounted for $9.1 billion of the import increase. Crude oil was up $3.3 billion and nonmonetary gold $3.1 billion. Capital goods imports rose $6.2 billion, including $2.4 billion in semiconductors and $1.3 billion in other industrial machinery.
Real goods imports, in 2017 dollars, rose 4.1% to $267.7 billion, against a 5.4% nominal increase. Year to date, the goods and services deficit is down 19.9% from the same period in 2025, and total imports are up 4.4%.
“This month, it is the trade war with Canada, which every day is getting worse — causing prices to go up and uncertainty that creates massive disruption,” a transportation equipment respondent said. “Buying continues to get pushed out indefinitely as customers don’t want to spend on capital expenditures until there is more certainty of costs and demand.”

A high-velocity drone launched at a disused Dutch airbase by the North Sea roars through the clouds and intercepts a mock enemy target detected by radar and verified using artificial intelligence.
The test by software company Intelic, which has a €30-million ($33.5-million) contract with the Dutch Defence Ministry to upgrade its air defenses, is an example of how technology is being developed and provided to Ukraine by European companies to help it defend itself against Russian attacks.
Amsterdam-based Intelic, one of scores of firms operating out of converted hangars at the airbase, now has an office in Kyiv and is helping Ukrainian forces as they face intensified Russian drone and missile barrages in a war in which drones have transformed the battlefield and driven rapid innovation.
In the test in late September, Intelic’s AI-powered software, Nexus, used multiple radars, sensors and cameras provided by other companies to identify the projectile as an enemy attack. A reconnaissance drone then verified it was an enemy drone with image recognition.
Although a human made the final decision to launch the AI-guided interceptor drone, the process could be fully autonomous, said Intelic CEO and founder Maurits Korthals Altes.
“Most of these systems use AI at the edge, so in the drone itself, to be able to hit a target, a flying drone for instance, and then actually get intercepted at high speeds,” he said.
“But you can also have AI for decision support,” for example by assisting a commander in the field, when there is sometimes a window of only a few seconds to decide whether or not to fire on an incoming jet-propelled drone.
The integration between the different systems enables a commander to make such decisions quickly. At high speeds, Korthals Altes said, “you’re not so likely to hit it manually, and you need a more autonomous system.”
The Dutch government’s investment is part of a spending push by the NATO country, which has allocated about €1.4 billion since 2022 to Ukraine’s drone program, making it one of Europe’s leading contributors along with Germany and Britain, figures from the Kiel Institute in Germany show.
‘CONNECTING TISSUE’
Since 2022, the Netherlands has provided military aid to Ukraine worth more than €12.5 billion, including nearly 1 million drones, the Defence Ministry said.
The Kiel Institute, which tracks military spending in Ukraine, said European aid for drones had jumped from €400 million in 2022, the year of Russia’s full-scale invasion, to €1.2 billion in 2025. The figure rose to €1.6 billion in the first four months of 2026 alone, it said.
Kyiv has increasingly sought support from allies to boost its air defenses, but European companies provide many different types of drones, which do not always “talk” to each other.
“Right now in Europe, there are over 700 drone manufacturers, and if we want to stay sovereign within Europe, we need to be able to have a system that is the connecting tissue between those different systems,” said Anika Kempter, a senior software engineer at Intelic.
She said Ukrainian brigades “might have different drones of different types from different vendors with different screens. Nexus solves this problem. So they can connect all of their drones in one system.”
DRONE TECHNOLOGY RACE
During the airbase test, engineers hovered over screens in a mobile command post using an interface that for the first time brings together radar target detection, AI verification and interceptor drones. Each component could be individually selected and operated from the single control panel.
Intelic’s command-and-control system is being rolled out on Ukraine’s battlefield, where operational decisions are sometimes still communicated via chat apps or phone calls. It supplements Delta, Ukraine’s own advanced battlefield management system.
Replacing human communication with autonomous systems shaves minutes off the time between when a drone is detected and forces try to shoot it down, potentially meaning the difference between life and death, Kempter said.
Russia now uses jet-propelled attack drones that fly at high altitude. In the first three weeks of September, Russia launched 2,100 such drones and 136 ​missiles at Ukraine, killing 288 people, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said.
Drone technology develops so quickly that air-defense hardware can rapidly become obsolete and need upgrading, but Intelic’s software can bridge the gap by adding new weapon systems to the platform, said Korthals Altes.
“That’s very important in an environment that’s unpredictable,” he said. “Because nobody really knows how a war or threat would look ... in two years. We have an idea, but we don’t know for sure. So that adaptability is key.”

Argenx shares have fallen more than 13% after the surprise futility finding, which overshadowed a mid-stage celiac disease win for a separate asset acquired in the company’s $2.2 billion Forte Biosciences buy.
Argenx is discontinuing a late-stage study of Vyvgart Hytrulo in Sjogren’s disease due to futility, a surprise setback that removes “the next potential blockbuster expansion opportunity” for the drug, William Blair analysts wrote on Thursday.
The biopharma is ending its Phase 3 UNITY trial after an independent data committee determined that the study would not meet its primary endpoint of improving systemic disease activity, according to a Thursday release .
As of market open, argenx’s stock had tumbled nearly 14%, or about $130 per share, resting at around $797 as of 11 a.m. ET.
UNITY had been evaluating argenx’s Vyvgart Hytrulo injection for Sjogren’s, an autoimmune disorder that most often affects moisture glands, with the most common symptoms of dry eyes and dry mouth. Vyvgart Hytrulo is currently approved to treat generalized myasthenia gravis and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy and recently scored a late-stage win in autoimmune myositis, a group of rare diseases that cause the immune system to attack the muscles.
Today’s futility announcement is surprising given that the trial results weren’t expected until the second half of 2027, William Blair wrote in a Thursday note.
Argenx told the firm that the futility analysis included data from more than 500 patients—as compared to the 630 enrolled—indicating that the review may have been conducted earlier than the primary endpoint assessment expected at week 48.
“Sjogren’s disease drug development has been bogged down by high placebo response rates, making it difficult to achieve robust separation versus placebo,” according to William Blair.
In argenx’s Phase 2 RHO study , the asset appeared differentiated in Sjogren’s compared to placebo at week 24. However, the study was underpowered and there was no difference compared to placebo in percentage of patients achieving at least a three-point improvement on an industry scale measuring disease activity, William Blair wrote.
The analysts had previously estimated peak sales of $1.4 billion in Sjogren’s but noted competition in the space, specifically from Novartis’ investigational monoclonal antibody ianalumab and Amgen’s CD40L antagonist fusion protein dazodalibep , both of which have recorded Phase 3 wins.

Volkswagen ID.4 hit with another battery recall
After recalling nearly 100,000 electric vehicles globally earlier this year over potential battery issues, including nearly 44,000 ID.4s in the US, Volkswagen’s electric SUV has been hit with another recall.

Kodiak AI and Charger USA have launched an autonomous trucking service between Dallas and Laredo, Texas , hauling refrigerated goods and dry freight on a 435-mile route. The companies announced the partnership on Thursday, with trucks already carrying loads for consumer goods and food and beverage customers.
What’s Related
The service runs between Charger’s terminals in the two cities. Kodiak and Charger completed their first delivery on September 8, making this Kodiak’s first route serving Laredo.
The trucks currently operate with a safety driver behind the wheel. The companies plan to remove the driver once Kodiak completes its safety case, a review of the evidence showing that its driving system can operate safely on the route.
Charger serves customers moving freight within the U.S. and across the Mexican border. The company offers refrigerated transport , truckload shipping , dedicated trucking, warehousing , and cross-border services.
RELATED: Aurora Triples Driverless Truck Routes Across Texas
Safety drivers remain in truck
Trucks on the Dallas-to-Laredo route use the Kodiak Driver, the company’s autonomous driving system. Charger and Kodiak expect to add more routes over time as Charger brings the technology into its own fleet.
“Charger came to us knowing what they wanted from autonomy and what they need to see before scaling it,” said Don Burnette, founder and CEO of Kodiak.
Kodiak provides its system as a service for customer-owned and operated trucks. That approach allows carriers such as Charger to bring autonomous driving into their existing trucking operations.
A new route to the border
Laredo handled more than $350 billion in international trade in 2025, accounting for nearly 40% of U.S. trade with Mexico, according to the announcement. Food, beverages, and other consumer goods moving through the area help replenish retail inventory.
The companies did not announce a date for removing safety drivers from the Dallas-to-Laredo route. Kodiak separately plans to launch long-haul driverless service by the end of 2026, with Dallas-to-Houston identified as its initial route.
Kodiak already has driverless trucks operating in the Permian Basin, where customer-owned vehicles have run without a driver since December 2024. The Dallas-to-Laredo partnership adds another Texas freight route as the company works toward driverless highway service.

A drone shot down by Genesis Arms Gen-12 SBM during exercise Falcon Peak at Cibola Site 17, Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona, Sept. 22, 2026. (Dept. of War photo by SSgt. Colten Tessness)
YUMA PROVING GROUND, Ariz. — As American servicemembers sweated in the Arizona desert, stress testing various counter-drone technologies, some senior officials had their minds thousands of miles away — thinking about how lessons gleaned here could help protect troops under US Central Command in the Middle East .
“Operating capabilities day after day in extreme desert conditions provides invaluable data on system durability and operator usability that directly translates to contested environments like the CENTCOM AO R [area of responsibility],” Marine Col. Scott Humr, deputy director of science and technology for the Army-led Joint Interagency Task Force (JIATF) 401 , told Breaking Defense last month shortly after the military concluded its most recent Falcon Peak exercise in Arizona desert.
He said the “realities of the desert” like intense heat, wind, dust and glare closely replicate the physical challenges faced by forces in CENTC OM in the Middle East. Handling such realities here in Yuma for Falcon Peak 26.2, put on by US Northern Command, allowed the team to “identify critical, highly practical sustainment needs that cannot be replicated in a laboratory.”
Related: Battling sand and wind, Pentagon evaluates counter-drone tech at southern border exercise
For instance, Humr said the task force had to pay close attention to how often solar panels powering the tech needed to be cleaned, as they would quickly become covered in dust. Soldiers had to make other “simple physical modifications” too, like getting new display shields so operators could read their screens in the unrelenting sunlight.
That information, in turn, can enable industry to better outfit troops in commands like CENTCOM.
“Passing this direct feedback from our operators back to developers ensures that counter-UAS [unmanned aerial systems] are fully ruggedized and optimized before they are deployed to forward combat environments,” he said.
Mike Wior, CEO of Allen Control Systems, the company that makes the counter-drone Bullfrog system, echoed Humr’s concerns over the wind. He told Breaking Defense on the sidelines of Falcon Peak that during the exercise his team had to adapt to the “gusts of wind that kind of come out of nowhere” and the crosswinds that affect the direction of the interceptors.
“That has been kind of an eye opener,” he said. “We’ve already been out there shooting for quite a while, and so we’ve been getting used to it. But it’s really, really good, comparable stuff to CENTCOM.”
The sentiment was echoed by Joe Cornelius, who’s firm Perseus makes drone interceptors that the company says cost under $5,000 a hit.
“Some of the big takeaways we took from [the exercise] were like, we need to do more robust testing on different wind environments and things like that.” Cornelius told Breaking Defense. “The winds out here at Yuma are about twice what we’ve ever tested with down in Texas. So that was a pretty big thing that we learned.”
Regarding the lessons learned related to tech, Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, JIATF-401’s commanding general, told reporters on Sept. 24 that the task force plans to inform leaders from CENTCOM of its success with constructing a “layered defense” during the exercis e — using different, overlapping defensive tech in a way that offers more than one chance to neutralize a threat. CENTCOM already uses layered defenses, but Ross said t hat beefing it up will be vital considering the ongoing risks Iranian Shaheed drones pose to US and allied bases in the region.
“We work in support of all the COCOMs, and so we and the services receive the requirements from them, and so we have provided support to [CENTCOM commander] Adm. [Brad] Cooper and CENTCOM,” Ross said. “I would say more than anything, [Falcon Peak] reinforced what we knew about the requirements for a counter-UAS ecosystem, meaning that we need a layered defense that consists of both active and passive sensing.”
He added that he’s seen how leaders in CENTCOM are “effectively” using the tools that are available, explaining that his task force’s role is to “try to give them some additional tools” so they can “layer them together in an effective manner to protect their critical assets.”
Though Ross didn’t specify what kind of tools could be offered to CENTCOM, during the exercise, the task force and NORTHCOM demoed three “lanes” of capabilities: sensing, kinetic interceptors (also known as drone-on-drone take downs) and ballistic take downs, which primarily consisted of small ammunition taking down the aircraft.
The Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) also played a role in finding relevant capabilities for CENTCOM during Falcon Peak. Angela Aspito, a director with DIU’s onramp hub in Arizona — which manages the continental US-based experimentation events for CENTCOM — told reporters DIU was successful in finding such capabilities, but she also did not specify on the types. But she said there are “gaps that we’re aware of that the warfighter needs to fill with technology.”
“It’s pretty relevant right now to be out in Arizona, getting everything that’s happening with the war in Iran and Epic Fury . There’s a lot of relevant capability that needs to be transitioned into the Middle East, and so the opportunity to see that on the battlefield today is really real,” Aspito said.

Novelis has produced the first aluminum coil on the cold mill at its $5 billion recycling and rolling plant in Bay Minette, Alabama. The company announced the milestone October 7 as it prepares to begin commercial shipments in the second quarter of 2027.
What’s Related
The plant is still being commissioned, with equipment needed for commercial shipments going through that process. Novelis is also working toward customer qualification, keeping the first-coil milestone separate from the start of regular shipments to buyers.
Steve Fisher, president and CEO of Novelis, described the milestone as “an important step in commissioning Bay Minette and increasing the supply of rolled aluminum in the United States.” He said the investment will help the company meet long-term demand in North America, where available aluminum production is constrained.
Fisher also said the project will increase the use of recycled material in Novelis products. The plant combines aluminum recycling and rolling at one location, bringing both operations together to supply customers in packaging , automotive manufacturing and other markets.
Shipments expected in 2027
Once fully operational, Bay Minette is expected to produce 600,000 metric tons of rolled aluminum annually. Its products will serve beverage packaging, automotive, and specialty-product customers, adding a large new source of U.S.-made aluminum for those buyers.
The April–June 2027 shipment target matches the company’s previously stated schedule, according to Aluminum Market Update. Novelis has already secured long-term customer agreements for the facility, according to its project website.
Recycling more than 15 billion cans a year
The facility includes a recycling center designed to process more than 15 billion used beverage cans annually. That operation will supply recycled material for the plant’s aluminum products alongside its new rolling equipment.
Novelis says Bay Minette is the first fully integrated aluminum recycling and rolling plant built in the United States in more than 40 years. The company expects the facility to create up to 1,000 new jobs once fully operational.

Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie October 8, 2026
Gold Mountain (ASX: GMN) is weighing the revival of a Brazilian tungsten mine that began during the Second World War after securing a 12-month exclusive right to acquire the property as Western governments scramble to diversify supplies of the strategic metal.
The Australian explorer has paid 1 million reais (C$284,000) for the right to acquire the 858-hectare Malhada do Angico property in northeastern Brazil’s Seridó Tungsten Province, according to an Oct. 5 announcement . A further 2 million reais would be payable if the transaction proceeds and receives regulatory approvals.
“GMN is excited by this tungsten opportunity, which I recently visited,” executive director David Evans said in the release. “We are fast tracking the exploration program and will commence drilling as soon as the necessary permits are obtained.”
The potential acquisition would expand Gold Mountain’s position in one of South America’s established tungsten-producing districts as China tightens control over exports and Western governments seek alternative sources for defence and industrial applications.
Gold Mountain shares closed 3.6% stronger at A5.7¢ in Sydney on Thursday. The stock has traded between A4.5¢ and A18.5¢ over the past year. Its market capitalization is A$16.7 million (C$16.5 million).
Historical workings
Malhada do Angico, about 10 km from Parelhas in Rio Grande do Norte state, began producing tungsten in 1942 and operated until 1982, according to a 1995 Brazilian mining engineering dissertation . The operation was sold to Companhia Industrial Fluminense in 1977, five years before its closure.
The operation extracted scheelite-bearing rock, a source of tungsten, from deposits formed where mineral-rich fluids altered surrounding rocks. The project lies within the Jucurutu Formation, which hosts several tungsten deposits, including the producing Brejuí mine, about 47 km north of Gold Mountain’s adjoining Logradouro tenements.
Gold Mountain has identified about 2 km of tungsten-bearing geological formations associated with the main historical workings, with another 2 km identified farther east. The company plans to test whether mineralization continues beneath the old workings.
Three rock-chip samples collected from Gold Mountain’s adjoining ground, mainly 300 to 600 metres along strike from Malhada do Angico, returned tungsten values exceeding the laboratory’s upper analytical limit of 10,000 parts per million, equivalent to more than 1.26% tungsten trioxide. The grab samples indicate mineralization but aren’t representative of the deposit’s overall grade.
The company has begun auger drilling of historical tailings to determine their grade and thickness and obtain samples for metallurgical testing. A separate diamond drilling program, awaiting permits, will test about 2 km of strike to depths of approximately 120 metres.
Gold Mountain is conducting technical, legal and regulatory due diligence before deciding whether to complete the acquisition. The mining application remains subject to a decision by Brazil’s National Mining Agency on an exploration report submitted in 2016.
Supply concerns
Tungsten is used in armour-piercing ammunition, cutting tools and high-temperature industrial components. Its strategic importance has grown as China, the dominant producer, has imposed export restrictions and Western governments have sought to reduce their dependence on Chinese supplies.
Tungsten prices have risen sharply amid constrained supplies and years of underinvestment, with BMO Capital Markets warning in February of a potential global shortage.
The European Union has also considered stockpiling tungsten , while the U.S. Department of Defense has committed $150 million to support the restart of Blue Moon Metals’ (TSXV: MOON; Nasdaq: BMM) Springer tungsten complex in Nevada.
For Gold Mountain, the immediate task is to establish whether the historical workings and tailings contain sufficient recoverable tungsten to justify further development. The company has yet to establish a mineral resource at Malhada do Angico or demonstrate the economic viability of restarting production.
